summary: On deep-space missions, crews cannot count on real-time medical support, and a black-box risk score is hard to trust when health is at stake. BASELINE is a web-based health monitoring system for the challenge “Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions”. It learns each astronaut’s own baseline from their first 14 readings. It then flags meaningful drift in vitals, sleep and fatigue, using smoothing, persistence checks (3 of the last 5 readings beyond 2 SD), fixed safety limits and multi-signal escalation. Every alert states what changed, which readings triggered it, why, and what action to consider. A Blood & Biomarkers module visualises real NASA OSDR Inspiration4 blood data (OSD-569) next to each crew member’s own pre-flight values. Every record is labelled by origin (NASA, simulated, user-entered or model-generated), and no clinical accuracy is claimed. BASELINE gives crews an early-warning layer they can audit instead of a score they must trust blindly.
details:
What it does. The app has JWT login and a mission profile. The dashboard shows a status of Normal, Monitor, Warning or Urgent Review. There are modules for vitals, cardiovascular, sleep and wellbeing, exercise, radiation and blood biomarkers, plus daily and weekly PDF reports.

How it works. The alert engine (alertEngine.js) runs five steps:

  1. Personal baseline (mean and SD of the first 14 readings).
  2. EWMA-smoothed z-score.
  3. Persistence rule.
  4. Hard safety limits.
  5. Escalation when 3 or more indicators move together, or 2 reach Warning.

If there is too little data it returns no alert rather than guessing. It has 6 unit tests.

Why it is creative.

  • Alerts explain themselves and use the person’s own baseline instead of population cut-offs.
  • Provenance is part of the data model: nasa_osdr | simulated | user_entered | model_generated.
  • It chose rules over ML on purpose, because 4 participants cannot honestly train or validate a model.
  • It surfaces data problems in the UI, for example the hemoglobin column labelled “percent” whose values look like g/dL.

Intended impact. Transparent decision support that helps crews and flight surgeons notice slow drift early, which matters most when ground contact is delayed.

Tools. React 18, Vite, Tailwind, Recharts, Node/Express-style serverless API, MongoDB Atlas with Mongoose, JWT with bcryptjs, Python/pandas for data import, GitHub, Vercel.

Factors considered. Alert fatigue (persistence rule), explainability, data honesty, missing values kept missing, and no fabricated NASA measurements.
dataRefs: NASA Open Science Data Repository, OSD-569
projectRefs: Sanders et al., “Inspiration4 data access through the NASA Open Science Data Repository,” npj Microgravity 2024
